blurb.deleteentitydialog: Delete confirmation with the entity's name, so you don't hit the wrong target.
blurb.impactpreviewdialog: Show what will be affected before applying a cascading change.

blurb.grouppopover: Anchored popover to edit or choose without losing the background context.
blurb.commandpalette: Action search and keyboard navigation (⌘K), command-palette style.

blurb.message: Inline notice within the flow: info, success, warning, or error.

type.title: Typography
type.lead: A rounded scale in rem on a 16 root (font-size-300 = 16px = exactly 1rem), step-named (the same language as the Pro Kit and the devs) and decoupled from the spacing scale. 8 sizes + 7 line heights.
type.note: 14 and 16 are not the same. The DS doesn't override the browser root (html stays at 100%), so 1rem = 16px and the ramp lands on round pixels. The 14 you see across the system is the other axis: it's the base of the spacing scale (--sc-scale-1 = 14px, the suffix is the multiplier) and the default body size (font-size-200). Dropping the root to 14 would shrink both axes at once.
type.foot: Named by step (100…800), not by value: the name doesn't lie if the value changes, and Figma, code, and the devs speak the same language. In rem so text scales with the browser's base size (accessibility). CSS also has font-size-50/75/600/700/900: these are snaps, steps the Kit doesn't ship that stick to their neighbor so step naming leaves no gaps.

applies.title: When to apply the class
applies.lead: Text styles apply to whatever is not a component. A DS component already publishes its typography through the PrimeNG theme; putting a class on top disconnects it from that theme, which is exactly what makes a token change reach every component on its own.
applies.yes_labels: Labels and supporting text owned by the screen (.sc-text-caption-regular)
applies.yes_tables: Headers and cells of a table you build yourself in HTML
applies.no_ds: Nothing inside an <sc-*>: its typography belongs to the component
applies.no_primeng: Nothing with a .p-* class: the preset paints it, in its own layer
applies.no_icons: Icons: <sc-icon> has its own size scale
applies.note: Measured on the Supervisor mockup: of its 43 texts, the 25 page-level ones carry an anchored style and the 18 living inside a component carry none. If you need a component to look different, move the token; do not put a class on top of it.

patterns.title: Screen patterns
patterns.lead: The quality bar when building a product screen. Each pattern points to what the system already solves, so a new screen is born consistent instead of being fixed afterward.

demo.title: Loading state: the contrast, live
demo.lead: On the left, sc-skeleton with the row's silhouette: it reserves the exact space, so nothing jumps when it loads. On the right, the centered spinner: it reserves no structure, and the layout jumps when the data finally arrives.

patterns.foot: It's the same bar followed by whoever builds this repo's apps: it's also in AGENTS.md (the «Screen UX» section), the document you read when you touch the code. It's not a checklist to show off, it's what separates a professional screen from a generic one.

color.title: Functional color
color.apply: Every color comes from a --sc-* token and means something: state, hierarchy, or feedback.
color.avoid: Hand-written hex, tinting buttons and icons for decoration, or using a --sc-color-* palette value as a page or background color: it doesn't flip in dark mode and becomes unreadable.
color.have: The --sc-* scale and the bridge to the preset. You never need a hex.

loading.title: Loading states
loading.apply: While data arrives, paint a skeleton shaped like the content and reserve its space.
loading.avoid: A centered spinner, or injecting data and letting the page jump (layout shift).
loading.have: sc-skeleton (rectangle or circle, wave animation). Live example below.

copy.title: Copy without filler
copy.apply: A title that explains itself stands alone. A description only if it adds something non-obvious.
copy.avoid: A decorative one- or two-sentence subtitle under every heading.
copy.have: A rule, not a component: less text, more signal. If removing it loses nothing, remove it.

icons.title: Consistent iconography
icons.apply: A single professional library, always via sc-icon (Material Symbols).
icons.avoid: Emojis in the interface, or mixing two icon sets.
icons.have: sc-icon over the generated set: one visual language across every app.

density.title: Density and hierarchy
density.apply: Compact layout. Secondary actions in a kebab menu, aligned metrics, chips reduced to an icon when color already states the status.
density.avoid: Repeating in every view the KPIs already on the dashboard, or cards with no data or action.
density.have: sc-datatable, sc-card, and the supervisor's overflow pattern.

a11y.title: Accessibility, the minimum bar
a11y.apply: 4.5:1 contrast on text and 3:1 on large text and icons. Every control reachable by keyboard, with visible focus and a label.
a11y.avoid: Signaling a state with color alone, or leaving a control without a label.
a11y.have: Contrast already lives in the tokens; the risk enters when you paint a color by hand.

motion.title: No jumps
motion.apply: Animate only transform and opacity. Images with width/height or aspect-ratio. Banners and toasts in already-reserved space.
motion.avoid: Animating top, left, width, or height, or inserting something over the content on load.
motion.have: The site's own theme transition already crossfades with opacity, without repositioning anything.

reglas.title: Rules system
reglas.lead: The rules system was rebuilt from scratch. Before: recording calls, with priorities, conflicts, and drafts. Now: transcribing, with several active rules and no conflicts, and a builder anyone understands. Each change is told with its before, its now, and its why. The screenshots are from the real Supervisor.

toc.p3: Scope: from checkboxes to a tree
toc.p4: Priority and conflicts: from hard to nothing

s1.title: First, what a rule is
s1.p1: A rule automates what happens to conversations that come in from now on: whether they're transcribed and whether they're analyzed with AI. It doesn't touch what already exists.
s1.note: Touching what already exists is something else: bulk actions (transcribe a selection now). Rule = future. Bulk = now. It's the easiest confusion to fall into, so it's worth pinning down before starting.

s2.title: The pivot: from recording to transcribing
s2.p1: For a long time, the strong case was recording rules. A change in regulations left them pointless, so they're out of the MVP. The legal detail stays out; what matters here is the consequence.
s2.p2: The weight shifted to transcription and classification, just as the multi-segment transcription system enters development. Rebuilding the rules to transcribe was the chance to simplify what had grown complicated. The three changes ahead are that simplification.

s3.title: Scope: from three rigid checkboxes to a tree
s3.lead: «Scope» is which conversations a rule reaches. It was the most rigid part of the old model, and where the change showed the most.
s3.altBefore: Old rule-creation screen: three checkbox groups, Services AND Groups AND Agents
s3.altAfter: New builder: a condition tree field·operator·value — AND within each alternative, OR between alternatives
s3.capAfter: A condition tree field · operator · value: AND within each alternative, OR between alternatives.
s3.why: The three boxes couldn't say normal business things: «sales or incidents», or mixing conditions. And they stored names: if you renamed a group or changed its members, the rule was left staring at an old name. The tree expresses any combination, and stores live references: «All» also includes whatever gets created tomorrow, and a group in the Agent field means «its members now».

s4.title: Priority and conflicts: from the hardest part to nothing
s4.lead: This is where all the old system's complexity lived. And the way to solve it was, simply, to make it disappear.
s4.altBefore: Old list: a priority column, two rules IN CONFLICT, a drafts section
s4.capBefore: Several active, ordered by priority, with two marked IN CONFLICT.
s4.altAfter: New list: no priority or conflicts, the state active or inactive per row
s4.capAfter: Several can be active. No priority numbers, no conflicts.
s4.why: Before, with several active rules, when two could apply to the same conversation you had to decide which one wins: a priority number, drag to reorder, and a detector that warned you of every clash. It was the most complex part of all. Now several can still be active, but the mess disappears with one simple idea: a conversation is processed only once, applying the union of what the matching rules ask for. No deciding who wins, no ordering, no conflicts. Turning one on no longer turns the others off.

s5.title: Drafts: one state fewer
s5.lead: The old list had an intermediate state nobody had asked for. It was removed.
s5.altBefore: Old list with an «Inactive and drafts» section and an UNEDITED DRAFT
s5.capBefore: Active, inactive… and «Unedited draft», in its own section.
s5.altAfter: New list with only two states: active or inactive
s5.capAfter: Two states and that's it: active or inactive.
s5.why: The «draft» was an unedited copy that couldn't be activated until you touched it, and it lived in a separate section. One extra state that only confused. Now deactivating a rule just moves it to Inactive (no copies or drafts), and duplicating creates a normal inactive copy, ready to edit or activate. Activate and deactivate is all a supervisor needs.

s6.title: What was gained: a live estimate
s6.p1: It wasn't all about removing. While you build a rule, a panel pinned to the right tells you how many conversations it would affect: «Would affect N of the last M conversations», with a proportion bar (broad vs. surgical) and a projection «≈ N a day». It's an estimate over the history, not a fixed figure. It really counts how many conversations match.
s6.note: And it guides without getting in the way: when you try to save, an incomplete condition or an impossible range is flagged and blocks; a duplicate or a contradiction only warns.

s7.title: Where they live: Repositories
s7.p1: Rules live in Repositories, inside administration, the same place as services, groups, or typifications. It's a simple table: name, the scope in prose, what it does, and its state. That phrase in the list («Applies when the service is Ventas Comercial and the duration is over 60s») comes straight from the condition tree, so you can read what a rule does without opening it.

s8.title: Transcription in detail
s8.p1: What multi-segment transcription is: a single conversation (a call) can have several recording segments, and each segment is transcribed separately. That's why a call with N segments counts as N audios, and each segment carries its own transcription state.
s8.p2: This lives on the Conversations side (the multi-segment player and the bulk actions), not in the rule builder: the rule decides what gets transcribed going forward; the segments are how what's already transcribed is stored and managed.
s8.part1: The base is already in the code: the multi-segment player and the per-segment state (transcribed or not) already exist, and the transcription bulk already counts the segments.
s8.part2: Cost: the bulk already counts how many audios come in and how many allow AI analysis (a separate toggle). The cost is real and grows with multi-segment.
s8.part3: Re-transcribing is destructive: it deletes the transcription and the derived analyses. That's why it asks for a written confirmation.

s9.title: What's left to close
s9.p1: The questions the MVP deliberately leaves open. Below, what's already been decided.

outcome.title: Conclusions
outcome.intro: What was decided and what's already been built since. What stayed up in the air goes at the end.

reglas.footer: This page lives inside sc-docs: it updates with the code. The «now» screenshots regenerate with npm run usage:capture, and the «before» ones stay saved to tell the change.

cost.detail: Each transcription consumes compute, and the AI analysis is separate. The cost grows with multi-segment transcription. Do we set limits? Is AI always optional? The builder already estimates the impact, but the cost is for the team to close.

governance.detail: If a conversation has several segments transcribed separately, which rule governs each one? How are they stored? When is it re-transcribed?

dependency.detail: AI classification needs the transcription underneath. If the transcription fails or doesn't exist, what does the classification rule do?

migration.detail: They become obsolete with the new law and leave the MVP. Do we auto-deactivate, delete, or convert them? And what happens to what's already recorded?

retention.detail: How long transcriptions are kept and how they're deleted. The regulatory change is what shifts the focus; the legal detail is for the team to close.

calendar.detail: Rules are configured by supervisors, from the Supervisor. It's still to be set when the multi-segment transcription system goes into production.

manyActive.t: Several active rules, no conflicts · done
manyActive.d: Several rules can be active at once; turning one on doesn't turn the others off. And without the old complexity: a conversation is processed once, applying the union of what the matching rules ask for. No priority, no ordering, no conflicts to resolve.

scope.t: Scope combines with AND and OR · done
scope.d: Within an alternative, conditions combine with AND; adding another alternative is the OR. That fixed structure expresses any combination with no switches to learn. Typification is just another entity (not a loose condition) and it's the clearest value case: «I only want the ones that ended in a sale».

liveRefs.t: Live references, not frozen names · done
liveRefs.d: «All» also includes future entities, and a group in the Agent field means «its members now». Changing a group's composition is reflected without re-editing the rule.

directionDuration.t: Direction and duration, inside the builder · done
directionDuration.d: They're just more scope fields, not a separate «Criteria» block. One place to filter, without duplicating direction in two spots.

estimate.d: As you build, the footer says «would affect N of the last M conversations», with a proportion bar and a day/month projection. It's an estimate over the history, not a fixed figure.

oneOrZero.t: A conversation meets the condition or it doesn't · decided
oneOrZero.d: One or zero: there's no partial match, nothing gets transcribed «for a piece» of the condition. And even if it fits several active rules, it's processed once: there's never a double transcription.

repos.t: The rules' home: Repositories · in progress
repos.d: In administration, not a modal: it's a form and reads better full-screen. The same repository serves transcription and typification rules, and later the IVR source lists (which today have to be replicated by hand across 15-16 nodes). Start simple, with a table.

futureFirst.t: Rules are forward-looking; classification comes later · decided
futureFirst.d: Nothing retroactive here: applying to past conversations is bulk. And AI classification (categories) is the highest-value part, but it's pulled out of here for now: transcription first.

pending.backend: Close with the backend team which criteria come in first; the builder already covers direction, duration, and typification. The backend can run ahead of the UI: create the table, add rules, and evaluate the condition even if the screen doesn't exist yet.
pending.transcription: Confirm the fine-tuning of transcription quality and effort (feasibility and cost). Today it cleans up music and noise by default.
pending.repos: Stand up the Repositories section (transcription + typification), starting with a simple table.
pending.simulator: Build the cost simulator: estimate what percentage would be transcribed and the spend, comparing with the previous month.
pending.aed: Advance AED with typification, schedules, and the transcription rule (including migrating the recording rules).

confirm.naming: Final naming of the entities («callers» vs. groups/ACD).
confirm.invert: Whether the option to invert or exclude a condition («all of this except X») comes in.
confirm.nested: A nested builder beyond 2 levels, and an impact/cost simulator as an evolution, not MVP.
confirm.detailWindow: The conversation detail in its own window (a non-blocking player).

feedback.title: Feedback
feedback.hint: Review notes, by date (most recent first). Each point validated against the prototype.

manyActive.d: The «only one active» limit is lifted: now several can be on. The overlap is resolved with no priority or conflicts, using the union rule: a conversation is processed once, applying what the matching rules ask for together. Along the way, the pending «silently deactivate» disappears.

pause.d: Today there's only Active/Inactive (a boolean). Add «Pause» as its own action, distinct from deactivating, for later.

header.d: Save lives at the bottom, in the footer; the header (back + title + type) is projected into the TopBar. The primary action ends up far from the navigation and can overlap with the app's breadcrumb. Resolve where navigation and Save live.

scopeCopy.d: It shows the tree's full prose (service + group + typification + duration): it can come out long and confusing in a cell. The list has NO description column today: decide whether name + short description is worth it, or shortening the prose with a tooltip.

exclusive.d: Understand whether, once you check Groups, you shouldn't be able to pick Services. Today they're NOT exclusive: service/group/agent combine freely with AND/OR in the tree. Decide whether there should be a cascade or exclusion (ties into «invert/exclude condition», already in To confirm).

oneTable.d: Unify the two sections into one table: the Status column already distinguishes Active/Inactive. Less noise. (Written under the «only one active» model of the time; that limit was lifted on Jul 17 — the single table still stands.)

confirmModal.t: Confirmation modal on activate — resolved Jul 17
confirmModal.d: Back then, activating a rule deactivated the previous one SILENTLY and asked for a confirmation «this will deactivate [X]». With several active at once (Jul 17), nothing is deactivated on activate: the modal is no longer needed.
